archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (aging core)
archetype.definition: A Pittsburgh team that wins the 5-on-5 chance battle by a real margin but sits sixth in the Metropolitan because its goaltending, finishing and close-game luck have all broken the wrong way.

report.headline: Penguins out-chance teams and lose anyway; goaltending and finishing owe them points.
report.take:
At 7-11-2 and 24th on the site, Pittsburgh looks like a lottery team, and the 82-game pace of 66 points says the same. The process numbers disagree. The Penguins own 52.4% of the 5-on-5 expected goals (11th) and 52% of the shot attempts (8th). That is a playoff-caliber territorial profile. The gap between that and a -0.45 Goal Diff / GP (24th) comes from three sources that usually do not last. The first is a 5-on-5 PDO of 97.7, well under the 100 baseline. The second is a team save % of .882 (25th). The third is a Pts vs Goal Diff of -3.5 (29th), so they have also come out on the wrong end of the coin-flip games.

The structural problems are real too, though. The forwards grade a D, and the ice-time list explains it. Sidney Crosby sits 102nd of 240 centers and is -7. Ben Kindel plays 17.43 minutes a night as a -12 with a sub-50% xGF. Evgeni Malkin (17 points in 18 games, the best Game Score on the team) and Tommy Novak (8 goals) are carrying the scoring. Nick Robertson's 7 goals with no assists in third-line minutes is a finishing streak, not a role. The blueline is the strength at a B. Kris Letang's 56.7% xGF anchors it, while Erik Karlsson's 19 points sit beside a 46.7% xGF and a -11, an offense-for-defense trade the team is currently losing.

The numbers also hide a split between 5-on-5 and all situations. At even strength the Penguins drive play. Across all situations their 27.1 shots a game (18th) trail the 27.9 they allow (19th). A power play converting 20% (22nd, below the league's 22.2%) does not add enough to cover that. Last year's 98-point team was the opposite case: it ranked 3rd in offense on a 101.2 PDO with a thinner 51% xGF. This year's team plays better and finishes worse.

Where it heads depends mostly on the crease. Arturs Silovs has started 12 games at .873 with a -2.3 GSAx. Sergei Murashov has been closer to average at .893. Average goaltending and normal shooting luck should turn this into a roughly .500 team the rest of the way. That is enough to escape the bottom of the league, but probably not enough to climb into a playoff spot from this hole.

strengths.title: Winning the 5-on-5 chance battle
strengths.body: Pittsburgh owns a clear majority of both the expected goals and the shot attempts at even strength, which puts it in the league's upper third on process. Much of it comes from the back end. Letang, Korczak and Stastney all sit near or above 55% xGF, and the depth centers Dewar and Lizotte are above 55% as well. History says this lasts: the Penguins have been at or above 51% CF in every one of the last five seasons.

strengths.title: Malkin and Novak driving the offense
strengths.body: Malkin has 17 points in 18 games and leads the forwards in Game Score. Novak has 8 goals in 15.6 minutes a night. Both are above 54% xGF, so the production comes with real territorial play behind it. Malkin's per-game rate is the one most likely to soften over a full season.

strengths.title: A penalty kill above league average
strengths.body: The kill is converting 79.6%, 13th and above the league's 77.4%. That is a better mark than they managed in 2024-25. It is not elite, but it is one phase of the game that is not costing them.

concerns.title: Goaltending below average in the crease
concerns.body: A combined .882 save % ranks 25th, and the goalies grade a D+. Silovs has taken the larger share of starts at .873 with a -2.3 GSAx. The team-level GSAx of -0.1 suggests the problem is more about poor results than a collapse, so some recovery is likely. Still, neither goalie has yet shown he can steal games.

concerns.title: Forward depth grades a D
concerns.body: Beyond Malkin, Novak and Rakell, the forward minutes go to players ranked in the bottom half of their tabs. Crosby is 102nd of 240 centers, and Kindel is 134th with a -12. Wingers against Pittsburgh are scoring well above expectation (26th), which points to the same forward group losing its defensive matchups. This is a talent issue more than a luck issue.

concerns.title: Offense fading into November
concerns.body: Scoring fell to 2.5 a game in November, and the last five games produced 2.6 a game against 3.8 allowed. The power play at 20% is not filling the gap, and team shooting is 10.9%, below the league's 11.4%. Some of the shooting slump should correct. A weak power play with this personnel is more worrying.

trend.note: October was a losing month with goals coming, and November has been worse on both ends. The last five games run at a -1.2 per-game differential against -0.45 for the season, even though the 5-on-5 underlying numbers have held.

weekAhead.headline: Three low-scoring opponents, two elite goalies, one road back-to-back.
weekAhead.body:
The schedule is a home game against St. Louis, then a road back-to-back at Nashville and Dallas. None of the three scores much: offense ranks of 26th, 21st and 23rd. That gives Pittsburgh's shaky goaltending a softer test than usual. The problem is the other end. Nashville's goalies lead the league's elite with a 12.4 GSAx and the No. 1 penalty kill at 90%. Dallas allows just 23.3 shots a game (3rd) behind A-graded goaltending. For a team whose problem is finishing, that is a bad pair of opponents.

St. Louis is the game to bank. The Blues are 9-9-2 with D+ defense and give up 28.6 shots a game, and their B+ goaltending is the only real obstacle. Nashville is more beatable than its record suggests: it sits at 46% CF (28th) and 48.4% xGF, so Pittsburgh should control play there. Whether that turns into goals against a hot goalie is the question of the week. Two points of three feels like the realistic target, with a sweep of the road trip unlikely on the back-to-back.

keyMatchups.title: Power play against Nashville's kill
keyMatchups.body: Pittsburgh's 20% power play meets the league's best kill at 90%. Nashville's goalies are also 2nd in GSAx, so even-strength chances may not convert either. Pittsburgh's possession edge has to come through at 5-on-5.

keyMatchups.title: Getting shots through Dallas
keyMatchups.body: Dallas allows 23.3 shots a game (3rd) and holds forwards well under their expected points (3rd). On the second night of a back-to-back, Pittsburgh's middling 27.1 shots a game will be squeezed. Expect a low-event game decided by one or two goals.

keyMatchups.title: St. Louis centers against Pittsburgh's middle
keyMatchups.body: The Blues' defense lets centers score above expectation (24th), and Pittsburgh's scoring runs through Malkin and Novak down the middle. Their blueline grades a D+ and allows 28.6 shots a game. This is the best chance all week for the offense to get going.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts the back-to-back in net, and whether Silovs' save % starts climbing toward Murashov's.

restOfSeason.body:
The xGF and CF shares are the most stable numbers on this sheet, and they say the Penguins are a slightly above-average 5-on-5 team. The PDO of 97.7, the 29th-ranked Pts vs Goal Diff and the .882 save % are the least stable, and all three should drift back toward normal. That points to something like .500-plus hockey over the last 62 games, a meaningful step up from the current 66-point pace. I project 76-86 final standings points and 31-37 wins.

What will not regress is the forward group's lack of depth, a power play below league average and a goaltending tandem without a clear standout. Those cap the rebound. Starting sixth in a division where Carolina and New Jersey are already pulling away, even a good run probably lands Pittsburgh just short of the bubble. Last season's 98 points came with a 101.2 PDO this roster is unlikely to repeat. Expect goals against to settle around 3.0-3.3 a game as the save % recovers.
swingFactors: Silovs' save % returning to league average
Power play converting with Malkin and Karlsson
Crosby's line turning possession into goals

confidence.note: 20 games; strong 5-on-5 process, but luck-driven numbers are still noisy.
